items.title: 67251_Chuck Green oral history interview
items.q: I hadn't seen Mr. Bill Bojangles Robinson till up to that time, see. He was having like his 52nd birthday, I think it was, at the RKO Palace in Boston... So that's what we did. We went over there, he liked company, see, Bojangles, so he starts to talking and asking questions.

ctx.x: So tap dancing really was a form of making people -- a dance form that was geared toward making people forget where they came from, bringing them into something different, making them happy.

It was on the rise. It was the most happy medium, tap dancing, see, because I mean Bojangles, he hadn't become the champion yet. He hadn't got into this at the Palace Theater, see? I mean there was vaudeville was here then, too. In the '30's. Vaudeville didn't go out until 1935. That was buried at the Palace Theater on Broadway, which was right there at -- where is that, 47th and Broadway -- and 7th Avenue, right? Now, see these tap dancers, you had people like Tom Patricola (PHONETIC), James Barton, Walter…
